questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A lambda with a single parameter can refer to it as `it`. `map` returns a new `List`, and `List.toString()` prints with brackets and commas, so the output is not space-separated or summed.

questions.question: What is the inferred type of `f`?
questions.explanation: The lambda takes one `Int` parameter and its last expression is a `String`, so its type is `(Int) -> String`. Parameter types go on the left of the arrow and the return type on the right. A plain lambda does not get a receiver type unless the expected type asks for one.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A lambda returns the value of its last expression, here `x + 1` = 6. The `x * 2` line is computed and then thrown away; nothing prints it.

questions.question: If a function's last parameter has a function type, you can pass the lambda outside the parentheses, and if the lambda is the only argument you can drop the parentheses entirely.
questions.explanation: This is trailing lambda syntax: `list.fold(0) { acc, x -> acc + x }` and `list.forEach { println(it) }`. It only works for the last parameter, which is why APIs put the function parameter last.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `::User` refers to the constructor as a `(String) -> User` function, so `map` builds one `User` per string. A data class `toString()` includes the property names, so it prints `name=ann` and not `User(ann)`.

questions.question: Why can you write `button.setOnClickListener { view -> openDetails() }` even though the method takes a `View.OnClickListener`?
options: `View.OnClickListener` is a single-method Java interface, so Kotlin applies SAM conversion
Kotlin generates an overload of `setOnClickListener` that takes `(View) -> Unit` for every Android method
`View.OnClickListener` is a Kotlin typealias for `(View) -> Unit`
The lambda is stored as `Any` and cast to `OnClickListener` at runtime
questions.explanation: Java interfaces with exactly one abstract method are SAM types, and Kotlin automatically turns a lambda into an implementation of one when it is passed as an argument. `OnClickListener` is a real Java interface, not a typealias, and no overloads are generated.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `multiplier` returns a lambda that remembers `factor`. `triple(4)` is 12 and `multiplier(2)(5)` calls the returned function straight away to get 10, so the sum is 22. Both are `Int`s, so `+` adds them rather than joining them as strings.

questions.question: Which of these can be assigned to a `val` of type `(Int, String) -> Unit`?
questions.explanation: `_` stands in for a parameter you don't use, but the lambda must still declare both parameters. `::log` has the matching type `(Int, String) -> Unit`. `it` only exists for lambdas with exactly one parameter, and `{ _ -> ... }` declares one parameter, so both fail to compile.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Each `makeCounter()` call creates a new `count`, and its lambda captures and changes that variable (Kotlin, unlike Java, lets a lambda modify a captured `var`). `a` has been called three times, so it returns 3. `b` has its own counter, so it returns 1.

questions.question: An adapter stores an optional callback. Which line inside `click` compiles and calls the callback only when it is set?
questions.explanation: A nullable function type has to be called with a safe call on `invoke`: `onItemClick?.invoke(item)`. Kotlin has no `?(...)` operator, and calling it directly (with or without `.invoke`) is rejected because the type is nullable.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `return@forEach` returns from the lambda only, so it skips the current element, like `continue`. It does not stop the loop or leave `main`, so the odd numbers print and then ` done`.

questions.question: You can pass a lambda to a parameter of type `Validator`, where `interface Validator { fun validate(s: String): Boolean }` is a plain Kotlin interface, without changing the declaration.
questions.explanation: SAM conversion for Kotlin interfaces only works when the interface is declared as `fun interface Validator`. With a plain `interface` you have to write `object : Validator { ... }`, or take a function type such as `(String) -> Boolean` instead. Java SAM interfaces don't need the keyword.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `::isLong` passes the top-level function as a predicate, and only "kotlin" (6 characters) is longer than 3. `String::length` then maps it to its length. "fun" has exactly 3 characters, so it doesn't pass `> 3`.

questions.question: What are the types of `a` and `b`?
questions.explanation: `g::greet` is a bound reference: the receiver `g` is already fixed, so only `msg` is left. `Greeter::greet` is unbound, so the receiver becomes the first parameter and you call it as `b(someGreeter, "Hi")`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Inside a `StringBuilder.() -> Unit` lambda, `this` is the builder, so `append` and `length` work without a qualifier. This is how `apply` and Kotlin DSLs work. `length` is read after "Hi" has been appended, so it is 2, not 0.

questions.question: The adapter takes `private val onItemClick: (Item) -> Unit`. Which line in `onBindViewHolder` calls the callback when the user taps the row?
questions.explanation: The listener lambda receives a `View`, so you call `onItemClick(item)` inside it. Passing `onItemClick` directly fails because the listener expects `(View) -> Unit`, not `(Item) -> Unit`. `{ view -> onItemClick }` compiles but only refers to the function without calling it, and calling `onItemClick(item)` outside the listener runs it during binding, not on a tap.

questions.question: Which call does NOT compile?
questions.explanation: `String.() -> Int` is the same function type as `(String) -> Int` with the receiver as the first argument, so `"hi".len()`, `len("hi")` and `len.invoke("hi")` all work. `len()` gives no receiver, so it fails with no value passed for the parameter.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Lambdas capture the variable, not its value at that moment. All three `while` lambdas share one `var i`, which is 3 by the time they run. A `for` loop creates a new `val j` on each iteration, so those lambdas print 0, 1 and 2.

questions.question: This program prints `BOB!`.
questions.code:
fun String.shout() = uppercase() + "!"

fun main() {
    var name = "Ann"
    val f = name::shout
    name = "Bob"
    println(f())
}
questions.explanation: A bound reference evaluates its receiver once, when the reference is created, so `f` holds the string "Ann" and prints `ANN!`. Reassigning `name` later doesn't affect it. A lambda `{ name.shout() }` would read the variable when called and print `BOB!`.

questions.question: Given `fun interface OnRefresh { fun refresh(force: Boolean) }`, which of these compile and create an `OnRefresh`?
options: object : OnRefresh { override fun refresh(force: Boolean) {} }
questions.explanation: A `fun interface` gets a SAM constructor that takes a lambda matching its single method `(Boolean) -> Unit`, so a named parameter and `it` both work, and so does an anonymous `object`. A two-parameter lambda doesn't match the method's signature, and `OnRefresh(true)` passes a value where a function is expected.
